name: Inframammary incision augmentation

lead: The inframammary (IMF) incision is one of the standard routes for placing breast implants. A cut of a few centimetres is made along the natural crease beneath the breast, so the scar sits in the fold and is usually hidden by the breast contour. People who choose breast augmentation use it to gain fuller, more projecting breasts and a more balanced figure.

Surgeons describe the approach as giving wide, direct access to the implant pocket, which allows precise placement and is workable for larger or silicone gel implants. Published studies compare it with periareolar and armpit (axillary) incisions for scarring, nipple sensation and complication rates.

paras: The procedure is done by a plastic surgeon under anaesthesia. The incision is made at the crease, the pocket is created above or below the chest muscle, the implant is placed, and the cut is closed. Patients typically choose the incision location in consultation with the surgeon, based on anatomy, implant type and scar preferences.

Risks are those of breast implant surgery generally, such as infection, bleeding, asymmetry, capsular contracture and the need for revision. The scar is in the fold and can be more or less noticeable depending on skin type, according to Wikipedia. Anyone considering it would discuss approach-specific trade-offs with a qualified surgeon.

angle.text: The IMF incision is a route for placing breast implants, so the cosmetic change comes from the implant itself. Its role is to give the surgeon wide access for positioning and to hide the scar in the natural fold.

lead: The inframammary incision is a surgical approach for breast augmentation in which the cut is made in the inframammary fold, the crease where the breast meets the chest. It is used to place implants for a larger, rounder or more symmetrical bust, and the resulting scar sits in the fold rather than on the breast surface [1].

Descriptions of the technique note that the long incision gives maximal access to the breast pocket, which supports precise implant positioning. Alternatives include the periareolar incision at the edge of the areola, the transaxillary route through the armpit, and the transumbilical route from the navel [1].

Research on the approach includes patient surveys and scar comparisons in augmentation, and a larger body of surgical series from breast reconstruction after nipple-sparing mastectomy, where incision placement affects nipple sensation and complication rates [2][3][4][5].
infobox: Surgical incision approach for breast implants
Along the fold; varies with skin type [1]

paras: In an IMF augmentation the surgeon cuts along the underside of the breast at the fold, opens a pocket for the implant, places it and closes the wound. The approach is described as offering maximal access to the interior of the breast, so the surgeon can see and control pocket dimensions [1].

The periareolar incision is shorter and sits at the areola border, which allows adjustment of the fold and combination with a lift, but makes large silicone implants harder to insert and carries a higher reported long-term risk of capsular contracture and possible damage to ducts and nipple nerves [1]. The transaxillary and transumbilical routes avoid cutting the breast skin but make precise placement technically harder [1]. The IMF, transaxillary and transumbilical approaches all avoid the nipple-areola complex [1].

A survey of 216 Chinese patients examined preferences and concerns about incision location for augmentation; the axillary approach is the dominant one in China, and patients were given structured education on the options before being asked [6].

A long-term follow-up study compared scars after axillary and inframammary fold incisions in Chinese patients [7]. A lateral inframammary approach has also been described for Asian augmentation mammaplasty [8].

sections.h: Use in reconstruction and nipple preservation
paras: Much of the published research on IMF incisions comes from nipple-sparing mastectomy with implant reconstruction. In a prospective nonrandomised trial of 97 analysed patients, nipple-areolar sensation was higher and sensory loss less frequent after IMF incisions than after periareolar or radial incisions [2]. A retrospective review of 181 prepectoral reconstructions found a higher rate of nipple-areolar complications with superior periareolar incisions than with IMF incisions [3].

Other series have compared incision types and complications [9], described a lateral IMF incision that avoids visible scars on the front of the breast [10], and compared IMF incisions with inverted-T incisions for ptotic versus non-ptotic breasts [4]. These populations are reconstruction patients, not cosmetic augmentation patients.

Human studies are mostly retrospective series and a few nonrandomised trials. They cover nipple sensation and complications by incision type after mastectomy [2][3][9], quality of life and complications by incision in ptotic and non-ptotic breasts [4], a patient survey and scar assessment in augmentation [6][7], and technique descriptions in feminizing chest surgery for gender-diverse patients [11]. A registered cohort study of 3,000 augmentation patients is examining implant displacement and rotation predictors [12].

Breast implant surgery carries general risks such as capsular contracture, asymmetry and revision surgery, and the choice of approach influences some of them [1]. Surgeons also weigh scar visibility, which can vary with skin type [1].
